title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
openingChapterLabel: Letter I — Walton to his Sister
openingText: You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings. I arrived here yesterday, and my first task is to assure my dear sister of my welfare and increasing confidence in the success of my undertaking.
about:
Frankenstein is the story of Victor Frankenstein, a young scientist who discovers how to create life from dead matter and assembles a being from corpses. Once awake, the creature is hideous, intelligent, and abandoned. He pursues his maker across Europe, demanding what he is owed. The novel is told as letters and nested narratives — first by an Arctic explorer, then by Frankenstein, then by the creature himself.

Mary Shelley was eighteen when she began writing it, twenty when it was published in 1818. She wrote it during a wet summer at Lake Geneva, in competition with her husband Percy and Lord Byron. The book is the founding text of science fiction and one of the founding texts of modern horror. It is also a serious moral argument about what creators owe what they have made.

angleCards.title: The creature as the moral centre.
angleCards.text: The creature's argument against Frankenstein — I did not ask to exist, you made me, you abandoned me — is the most coherent position in the novel. I want to read it asking whether Victor ever genuinely engages with it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Frankenstein with the creature as the moral centre — I want to follow his argument against Frankenstein, which I believe is the strongest argument in the novel, and understand what it means that Victor never answers it.

angleCards.title: The responsibility of creators.
angleCards.text: Frankenstein brings a conscious being into existence and then flees from it. I want to think through what he owed the creature he made — and what the novel proposes about the ethics of creation.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Frankenstein to think about the responsibility of creators — what Frankenstein owes the being he made, whether he ever fulfils that obligation, and what the novel proposes about the ethics of bringing a new being into existence.

angleCards.title: Shelley writing about ambition.
angleCards.text: Mary Shelley was 19 when she began this novel. Her mother died giving birth to her. Her own child died. I want to read Frankenstein knowing who wrote it and why the question of bringing life into being mattered so personally.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Frankenstein as a 19-year-old's warning about what happens when men pursue knowledge and creation without thinking about consequences — and I want to understand what Shelley, writing from her own experience, was working through.

angleCards.title: Horror or loneliness?
angleCards.text: The monster of popular culture is nothing like Shelley's creature — who reads Milton, learns French, and desperately wants friendship. I want to read this as a novel about loneliness and ask whether that is more frightening than any monster.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Frankenstein asking whether this is really a horror novel or a novel about loneliness — about what it means to be created without being wanted, to be intelligent without being recognised, to exist without belonging.

cast.name: Victor Frankenstein
cast.description: Obsessive, brilliant, and profoundly irresponsible. Creates life and immediately abandons it. Spends the rest of the novel being pursued by the consequences of that decision — and never quite accepting that he caused them.

cast.name: The Creature
cast.description: Intelligent, gentle at first, and utterly alone. Educates himself on Paradise Lost, Plutarch's Lives, and the Sorrows of Young Werther. His argument against Frankenstein is the most coherent in the novel.

cast.name: Walton
cast.description: An Arctic explorer with Frankenstein-like ambitions — seeking glory, pushing into danger, ignoring warning. He finds Victor dying in the ice. The novel opens and closes with his letters. He is not incidental.

cast.name: Elizabeth
cast.description: Victor's adopted sister and fiancée. The creature threatens her directly and Victor never takes it seriously enough. Her fate is the most damning evidence of Victor's failure to protect what he claims to love.

cast.name: Henry Clerval
cast.description: Victor's closest friend — warm, literary, interested in people. Everything Victor is not. He nurses Victor back to health twice. Victor never really sees him. His end is the novel's most bitter irony.

cast.name: De Lacey's Family
cast.description: The exiled French family the creature observes in secret for months. Through them he learns language, kindness, love, and grief. They are the only humans who have been kind to him — unknowingly.

acclaim.quote: It is no slight merit in our eyes, that the tale, though wild in incident, is written in plain and forcible English, without exhibiting that mixture of hyperbolical Germanisms with which tales of wonder are usually told.
acclaim.context: review in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, March 1818

whyItMatters.title: What Creators Owe What They Make
whyItMatters.body: The novel deals with whether a creator has obligations to a being he has called into existence. Victor abandons what he has made; the creature responds with violence. The argument echoes through every story we now tell about technology making things we cannot control.

whyItMatters.title: Two Voices, One Argument
whyItMatters.body: The book gives Victor and the creature equal narrative weight. We hear the creature's case in his own words — his loneliness, his self-education, his demand for a companion. The novel forces the reader to take seriously a being who would normally be treated as a monster.

whyItMatters.title: Science Reaching for What Religion Held
whyItMatters.body: Mary Shelley wrote at the moment when science began to reach into the things religion used to explain — life, death, the soul. The novel does not reject science but asks what it means when humans can do what gods used to do. The question has only become more pressing.
